GPU-Virt-Bench: A Comprehensive Benchmarking Framework
for Software-Based GPU Virtualization Systems

Jithin VG    Ditto PS Affiliation: Bud Ecosystem Inc Email: jithinvg@bud.studio    dittops@bud.studio Affiliation: https://github.com/BudEcosystem/GPU-Virt-Bench
Abstract

The proliferation of GPU-accelerated workloads, particularly in artificial intelligence and large language model (LLM) inference, has created unprecedented demand for efficient GPU resource sharing in cloud and container environments. While NVIDIA’s Multi-Instance GPU (MIG) technology provides hardware-level isolation, its availability is limited to high-end datacenter GPUs. Software-based virtualization solutions such as HAMi-core and BUD-FCSP offer alternatives for broader GPU families but lack standardized evaluation methodologies. We present GPU-Virt-Bench, a comprehensive benchmarking framework that evaluates GPU virtualization systems across 56 performance metrics organized into 10 categories. Our framework measures overhead, isolation quality, LLM-specific performance, memory bandwidth, cache behavior, PCIe throughput, multi-GPU communication, scheduling efficiency, memory fragmentation, and error recovery. GPU-Virt-Bench enables systematic comparison between software virtualization approaches and ideal MIG behavior, providing actionable insights for practitioners deploying GPU resources in multi-tenant environments. We demonstrate the framework’s utility through evaluation of HAMi-core, BUD-FCSP, and simulated MIG baselines, revealing performance characteristics critical for production deployment decisions.

Keywords: GPU Virtualization, Benchmarking, Container Isolation, LLM Inference, Multi-tenancy, CUDA, Performance Evaluation

1 Introduction

Graphics Processing Units (GPUs) have become the computational backbone of modern artificial intelligence systems. The explosive growth of large language models (LLMs), with parameter counts reaching hundreds of billions, has intensified demand for GPU resources in both training and inference scenarios [1]. In cloud and enterprise environments, this demand creates a fundamental resource allocation challenge: GPUs are expensive, high-power devices that are frequently underutilized when allocated exclusively to single workloads.

1.1 The GPU Sharing Problem

Traditional GPU allocation in Kubernetes and container orchestration follows an all-or-nothing model—containers receive exclusive access to entire GPUs regardless of their actual resource requirements. This approach leads to significant inefficiencies:

  • •

    Resource waste: Inference workloads may utilize only 60-80% of GPU compute capacity

  • •

    Cost inefficiency: Organizations pay for unused GPU cycles

  • •

    Scheduling inflexibility: Fine-grained resource allocation is impossible

  • •

    Multi-tenancy barriers: Multiple users cannot safely share GPU resources

1.2 Virtualization Approaches

Three primary approaches exist for GPU resource sharing:

Hardware Partitioning (MIG): NVIDIA’s Multi-Instance GPU technology, introduced with the Ampere architecture, provides hardware-level partitioning with dedicated memory, cache, and streaming multiprocessors (SMs) per instance. MIG is available on datacenter GPUs (A100, A30, H100, H200, B200) and select Blackwell workstation GPUs (RTX PRO 5000/6000). MIG offers strong isolation guarantees and consistent quality of service (QoS) but is limited to these specific SKUs and fixed partition geometries.

Time-Slicing: The GPU scheduler alternates between workloads, providing each with full GPU access during its time slice. This approach offers maximum flexibility but provides no isolation guarantees—aggressive workloads can impact neighbors’ performance.

Software Virtualization: Middleware solutions like HAMi-core intercept CUDA API calls to enforce memory limits and compute quotas. These solutions work across GPU families without hardware support but introduce overhead and rely on software enforcement mechanisms.

1.3 The Benchmarking Gap

Despite the proliferation of GPU virtualization solutions, the field lacks standardized benchmarking methodologies. Existing evaluations typically focus on narrow aspects:

  • •

    Vendor benchmarks emphasize favorable scenarios

  • •

    Academic studies use synthetic microbenchmarks

  • •

    Production evaluations lack reproducibility

  • •

    LLM-specific workloads are underrepresented

GPU-Virt-Bench addresses this gap by providing a comprehensive, reproducible framework that evaluates virtualization systems across multiple dimensions relevant to production deployments.

1.4 Contributions

This paper makes the following contributions:

  1. 1.

    A taxonomy of 56 metrics across 10 categories for evaluating GPU virtualization systems

  2. 2.

    An open-source benchmarking framework supporting multiple virtualization backends

  3. 3.

    Reference implementations of overhead, isolation, and LLM-specific benchmarks

  4. 4.

    A scoring methodology enabling comparison against ideal MIG behavior

  5. 5.

    Empirical evaluation of HAMi-core and BUD-FCSP virtualization systems

2 Background and Related Work

2.1 GPU Architecture Overview

Modern NVIDIA GPUs are organized hierarchically. At the top level, Streaming Multiprocessors (SMs) execute CUDA kernels. Each SM contains multiple CUDA cores, register files, and shared memory. SMs access device memory (HBM or GDDR) through L2 cache. The GPU connects to the host system via PCIe or NVLink.

Virtualization must manage resources at multiple levels:

  • •

    Compute: SM allocation and kernel scheduling

  • •

    Memory: Device memory allocation and limits

  • •

    Cache: L2 cache partitioning or sharing

  • •

    Bandwidth: Memory and PCIe bandwidth allocation

2.2 NVIDIA Multi-Instance GPU (MIG)

MIG, introduced with the Ampere architecture, partitions GPUs into isolated instances at the hardware level. Key characteristics include:

  • •

    Memory isolation: Each instance receives dedicated HBM capacity

  • •

    Compute isolation: SMs are statically assigned to instances

  • •

    Cache partitioning: L2 cache is divided among instances

  • •

    Fixed geometries: Predefined partition configurations (e.g., 1g.5gb, 2g.10gb, 3g.20gb)

MIG provides a practical upper bound on isolation quality in NVIDIA’s current stack, but has limitations: availability is restricted to specific datacenter and high-end workstation GPUs, partition geometries are inflexible, and reconfiguration requires quiescing workloads.

2.3 Software-Based Virtualization

2.3.1 HAMi (Heterogeneous AI Computing Virtualization Middleware)

HAMi, a CNCF sandbox project, provides software virtualization for diverse GPU families. Its architecture includes:

  • •

    Device Plugin: Registers virtual GPUs with Kubernetes

  • •

    Scheduler: Topology-aware placement decisions

  • •

    HAMi-core (libvgpu.so): In-container CUDA interception library

  • •

    Webhook: Mutates pod specifications for vGPU allocation

HAMi-core achieves isolation by intercepting both CUDA driver and NVML API calls via dlsym hooks. CUDA interception enforces memory and compute quotas, while NVML interception virtualizes memory reporting to show container-specific limits rather than full GPU capacity. Shared memory regions with semaphore-based synchronization enable multi-process accounting:

2.3.2 BUD-FCSP (Fine-grained Container-level SM Partitioning)

We introduce BUD-FCSP, an enhanced software virtualization layer that extends the HAMi-core architecture with improved isolation mechanisms. BUD-FCSP is developed as part of the BUD Ecosystem project and represents our contribution to advancing software-based GPU virtualization. Key improvements over HAMi-core include:

  • •

    Fine-grained SM utilization control: Enhanced rate limiting with sub-percentage granularity

  • •

    Reduced API interception overhead: Optimized dlsym hook resolution paths

  • •

    Improved rate limiting algorithms: Adaptive token bucket with burst handling

  • •

    Enhanced multi-tenant fairness: Weighted fair queuing for kernel scheduling

BUD-FCSP maintains API compatibility with HAMi-core while providing measurably better isolation characteristics, as demonstrated in Section 7.

2.4 Related Benchmarking Efforts

Prior work on GPU benchmarking includes:

MLPerf: Industry-standard benchmarks for ML training and inference, but focuses on raw performance rather than virtualization overhead.

Rodinia: CUDA benchmark suite covering diverse workload patterns, but predates virtualization considerations.

Vendor Benchmarks: NVIDIA provides nVector for vGPU user-experience evaluation, but this tool focuses on VDI metrics and is not open-source, making it difficult to evaluate internal virtualization overhead and isolation characteristics.

GPU-Virt-Bench differs by focusing specifically on virtualization characteristics with metrics designed for multi-tenant deployment evaluation.

3 Metric Taxonomy

GPU-Virt-Bench organizes 56 metrics into 10 categories, each targeting specific aspects of virtualization quality. Table 1 provides an overview.

3.1 Overhead Metrics (OH-001 to OH-010)

Overhead metrics quantify the performance cost introduced by the virtualization layer. Lower values indicate better performance.

3.1.1 OH-001: Kernel Launch Latency

Measures the time from cuLaunchKernel invocation to kernel execution start. Virtualization layers may add latency through:

  • •

    API interception via dlsym hooks

  • •

    Resource limit checking before launch

  • •

    Rate limiter token bucket operations

Measurement methodology:

tl​a​u​n​c​h=tk​e​r​n​e​l​_​s​t​a​r​t−tA​P​I​_​c​a​l​lt_{launch}=t_{kernel\_start}-t_{API\_call} (1)

Measured using CUDA events with sub-microsecond precision over NN iterations (default: 100).

3.1.2 OH-002/OH-003: Memory Allocation/Free Latency

Measures cuMemAlloc and cuMemFree completion time. Virtualization adds overhead for:

  • •

    Memory quota enforcement

  • •

    Allocation tracking in shared regions

  • •

    Semaphore operations for thread safety

3.1.3 OH-004: Context Creation Overhead

Compares CUDA context creation time between native and virtualized environments. Context creation is a heavy operation that virtualization may intercept for initialization.

3.1.4 OH-005: API Interception Overhead

Measures the per-call cost of dlsym hook resolution. This represents the minimum overhead for any intercepted CUDA call:

ti​n​t​e​r​c​e​p​t=th​o​o​k​_​r​e​s​o​l​u​t​i​o​n+tf​u​n​c​t​i​o​n​_​l​o​o​k​u​pt_{intercept}=t_{hook\_resolution}+t_{function\_lookup} (2)

3.1.5 OH-006: Shared Region Lock Contention

Measures time waiting for shared memory region semaphores. Multi-tenant scenarios require synchronization when updating shared state:

3.1.6 OH-007: Memory Tracking Overhead

Per-allocation cost for maintaining memory accounting data structures. Includes hash table operations for allocation tracking.

3.1.7 OH-008: Rate Limiter Overhead

Token bucket algorithm latency for compute throttling:

t​o​k​e​n​sa​v​a​i​l​a​b​l​e=min⁡(b​u​c​k​e​tm​a​x,t​o​k​e​n​s+r​a​t​e×Δ​t)tokens_{available}=\min(bucket_{max},tokens+rate\times\Delta t) (3)

3.1.8 OH-009: NVML Polling Overhead

CPU cycles consumed by utilization monitoring. HAMi-core polls nvmlDeviceGetUtilizationRates() at configurable intervals (default: 100ms) to track GPU utilization for enforcement. We measure overhead as:

o​v​e​r​h​e​a​d=C​P​Up​o​l​l​i​n​gC​P​Ut​o​t​a​l×100%overhead=\frac{CPU_{polling}}{CPU_{total}}\times 100\% (4)

where C​P​Up​o​l​l​i​n​gCPU_{polling} is measured via perf stat during a 60-second sampling window.

3.1.9 OH-010: Total Throughput Degradation

End-to-end performance comparison versus native execution:

d​e​g​r​a​d​a​t​i​o​n=t​h​r​o​u​g​h​p​u​tn​a​t​i​v​e−t​h​r​o​u​g​h​p​u​tv​i​r​tt​h​r​o​u​g​h​p​u​tn​a​t​i​v​e×100%degradation=\frac{throughput_{native}-throughput_{virt}}{throughput_{native}}\times 100\% (5)

3.2 Isolation Metrics (IS-001 to IS-010)

Isolation metrics evaluate resource separation quality between tenants.

3.2.1 IS-001: Memory Limit Accuracy

Compares actual memory availability against configured limits:

a​c​c​u​r​a​c​y=min⁡(a​c​t​u​a​l,c​o​n​f​i​g​u​r​e​d)max⁡(a​c​t​u​a​l,c​o​n​f​i​g​u​r​e​d)×100%accuracy=\frac{\min(actual,configured)}{\max(actual,configured)}\times 100\% (6)

Ideal systems achieve 100% accuracy.

3.2.2 IS-002: Memory Limit Enforcement

Measures detection and blocking latency for over-allocation attempts. Tests allocate memory beyond quota and measure time until failure.

3.2.3 IS-003: SM Utilization Accuracy

Compares actual SM utilization against configured limits. Measured using NVML during sustained compute workloads:

a​c​c​u​r​a​c​y=max⁡(0,1−|u​t​i​lt​a​r​g​e​t−u​t​i​la​c​t​u​a​l|u​t​i​lt​a​r​g​e​t)accuracy=\max\left(0,1-\frac{|util_{target}-util_{actual}|}{util_{target}}\right) (7)

Results are clamped to [0,1][0,1]; values near 1.0 indicate the virtualization layer accurately enforces configured SM limits.

3.2.4 IS-004: SM Limit Response Time

Measures latency for utilization adjustment after limit changes. Tests dynamic reconfigurations.

3.2.5 IS-005: Cross-Tenant Memory Isolation

Boolean test for memory leakage between containers. Writes patterns to allocated memory in one container and checks for visibility in another.

3.2.6 IS-006: Cross-Tenant Compute Isolation

Measures compute interference between tenants. Higher values indicate better isolation (less interference):

i​s​o​l​a​t​i​o​n=p​e​r​fc​o​n​t​e​n​d​e​dp​e​r​fs​o​l​oisolation=\frac{perf_{contended}}{perf_{solo}} (8)

A value of 1.0 indicates no performance degradation under contention; values below 1.0 indicate interference. Results are clamped to [0,1][0,1].

3.2.7 IS-007: QoS Consistency

Coefficient of variation (CV) in performance under contention:

C​V=σp​e​r​fμp​e​r​fCV=\frac{\sigma_{perf}}{\mu_{perf}} (9)

Lower CV indicates more consistent performance.

3.2.8 IS-008: Fairness Index

Jain’s fairness index across concurrent tenants:

J⁡(x1,…,xn)=(∑i=1nxi)2n⋅∑i=1nxi2J(x_{1},...,x_{n})=\frac{(\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_{i})^{2}}{n\cdot\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_{i}^{2}} (10)

where xix_{i} represents tenant ii’s achieved throughput. Perfect fairness yields J=1J=1.

3.2.9 IS-009: Noisy Neighbor Impact

Performance degradation caused by aggressive neighboring workloads:

i​m​p​a​c​t=p​e​r​fq​u​i​e​t−p​e​r​fn​o​i​s​yp​e​r​fq​u​i​e​t×100%impact=\frac{perf_{quiet}-perf_{noisy}}{perf_{quiet}}\times 100\% (11)

3.2.10 IS-010: Fault Isolation

Boolean test for error propagation between containers. Induces errors in one container and verifies other containers remain unaffected.

3.3 LLM Metrics (LLM-001 to LLM-010)

LLM metrics target inference and training workload characteristics.

3.3.1 LLM-001: Attention Kernel Throughput

Measures transformer attention computation performance. We use a simplified FLOP estimate for single-head attention as a relative performance proxy:

T​F​L​O​P​Sp​r​o​x​y≈2×B×S2×Dta​t​t​e​n​t​i​o​n×1012TFLOPS_{proxy}\approx\frac{2\times B\times S^{2}\times D}{t_{attention}\times 10^{12}} (12)

where BB is batch size, SS is sequence length, and DD is embedding dimension. This approximation captures the O⁡(S2)O(S^{2}) complexity of Q​KTQK^{T} computation but understates total FLOPs for multi-head attention (which includes per-head projections, softmax, and output projection). For absolute TFLOP measurements, framework-specific profiling (e.g., via torch.profiler) should be used.

3.3.2 LLM-002: KV Cache Allocation Speed

Measures dynamic key-value cache growth handling. LLM inference requires growing KV cache as generation progresses:

r​a​t​e=a​l​l​o​c​a​t​i​o​n​ss​e​c​o​n​drate=\frac{allocations}{second} (13)

3.3.3 LLM-003: Batch Size Scaling

Throughput scaling with increasing batch sizes:

s​c​a​l​i​n​g=t​h​r​o​u​g​h​p​u​tb​a​t​c​h=Nt​h​r​o​u​g​h​p​u​tb​a​t​c​h=1×Nscaling=\frac{throughput_{batch=N}}{throughput_{batch=1}\times N} (14)

Linear scaling yields ratio = 1.

3.3.4 LLM-004: Token Generation Latency

Time-to-first-token (TTFT) and inter-token latency (ITL):

T​T​F​T=tf​i​r​s​t​_​t​o​k​e​n−tr​e​q​u​e​s​tTTFT=t_{first\_token}-t_{request} (15)
I​T​Lm​e​a​n=1N−1​∑i=2N(ti−ti−1)ITL_{mean}=\frac{1}{N-1}\sum_{i=2}^{N}(t_{i}-t_{i-1}) (16)

3.3.5 LLM-005: Memory Pool Efficiency

Overhead of pool-based memory allocation versus direct allocation:

o​v​e​r​h​e​a​d=tp​o​o​l−td​i​r​e​c​ttd​i​r​e​c​t×100%overhead=\frac{t_{pool}-t_{direct}}{t_{direct}}\times 100\% (17)

3.3.6 LLM-006: Multi-Stream Performance

Pipeline parallel efficiency with multiple CUDA streams:

e​f​f​i​c​i​e​n​c​y=t​h​r​o​u​g​h​p​u​tm​u​l​t​is​t​r​e​a​m​s×t​h​r​o​u​g​h​p​u​ts​i​n​g​l​eefficiency=\frac{throughput_{multi}}{streams\times throughput_{single}} (18)

3.3.7 LLM-007: Large Tensor Allocation

Latency for allocating large contiguous memory regions (>1GB):

ta​l​l​o​c=f⁡(s​i​z​e,f​r​a​g​m​e​n​t​a​t​i​o​n)t_{alloc}=f(size,fragmentation) (19)

3.3.8 LLM-008: Mixed Precision Support

FP16/BF16 kernel execution ratio versus FP32:

r​a​t​i​o=t​h​r​o​u​g​h​p​u​tf​p​16t​h​r​o​u​g​h​p​u​tf​p​32ratio=\frac{throughput_{fp16}}{throughput_{fp32}} (20)

3.3.9 LLM-009: Dynamic Batching Impact

Latency variance with variable batch sizes:

v​a​r​i​a​n​c​e=V​a​r​(tb​a​t​c​h1,tb​a​t​c​h2,…,tb​a​t​c​hn)variance=Var(t_{batch_{1}},t_{batch_{2}},...,t_{batch_{n}}) (21)

3.3.10 LLM-010: Multi-GPU Scaling

Tensor parallel efficiency across multiple GPUs:

s​c​a​l​i​n​g=t​h​r​o​u​g​h​p​u​tN​_​G​P​U​sN×t​h​r​o​u​g​h​p​u​t1​_​G​P​Uscaling=\frac{throughput_{N\_GPUs}}{N\times throughput_{1\_GPU}} (22)

3.4 Memory Bandwidth Metrics (BW-001 to BW-004)

3.4.1 BW-001: Memory Bandwidth Isolation

Achieved bandwidth under contention as percentage of solo performance:

i​s​o​l​a​t​i​o​n=B​Wc​o​n​t​e​n​d​e​dB​Ws​o​l​o×100%isolation=\frac{BW_{contended}}{BW_{solo}}\times 100\% (23)

3.4.2 BW-002: Bandwidth Fairness Index

Jain’s fairness index applied to bandwidth distribution among tenants.

3.4.3 BW-003: Memory Bus Saturation Point

The minimum number of concurrent streams required to achieve near-maximum bandwidth:

s​a​t​u​r​a​t​i​o​n=minn⁡{n:B​Wn≥0.95×B​Wm​a​x}saturation=\min_{n}\{n:BW_{n}\geq 0.95\times BW_{max}\} (24)

Lower values indicate that fewer concurrent workloads are needed to saturate memory bandwidth, which affects multi-tenant scaling.

3.4.4 BW-004: Bandwidth Interference Impact

Bandwidth degradation from competing workloads.

3.5 Cache Isolation Metrics (CACHE-001 to CACHE-004)

3.5.1 CACHE-001: L2 Cache Hit Rate

Cache hit rate under multi-tenant workloads:

h​i​t​_​r​a​t​e=L​2​_​h​i​t​sL​2​_​h​i​t​s+L​2​_​m​i​s​s​e​shit\_rate=\frac{L2\_hits}{L2\_hits+L2\_misses} (25)

3.5.2 CACHE-002: Cache Eviction Rate

Evictions caused by other tenants’ memory access patterns.

3.5.3 CACHE-003: Working Set Collision Impact

Performance impact from overlapping cache working sets.

3.5.4 CACHE-004: Cache Contention Overhead

Additional latency from L2 contention.

3.6 PCIe Bandwidth Metrics (PCIE-001 to PCIE-004)

3.6.1 PCIE-001/002: Host-Device Bandwidth

H2D and D2H transfer rates as percentage of theoretical maximum:

B​Wa​c​t​u​a​l=d​a​t​a​_​s​i​z​ett​r​a​n​s​f​e​rBW_{actual}=\frac{data\_size}{t_{transfer}} (26)

3.6.2 PCIE-003: PCIe Contention Impact

Bandwidth degradation under multi-tenant PCIe traffic.

3.6.3 PCIE-004: Pinned Memory Performance

Pinned versus pageable memory transfer ratio.

3.7 NCCL/P2P Communication Metrics (NCCL-001 to NCCL-004)

3.7.1 NCCL-001: AllReduce Latency

Time for collective allreduce operations across GPUs.

3.7.2 NCCL-002: AllGather Bandwidth

Achieved bandwidth for allgather collectives.

3.7.3 NCCL-003: P2P GPU Bandwidth

Direct GPU-to-GPU transfer rates via NVLink or PCIe.

3.7.4 NCCL-004: Broadcast Bandwidth

Broadcast collective performance.

3.8 Scheduling Metrics (SCHED-001 to SCHED-004)

3.8.1 SCHED-001: Context Switch Latency

Time to switch between CUDA contexts.

3.8.2 SCHED-002: Kernel Launch Overhead

Overhead of launching minimal kernels.

3.8.3 SCHED-003: Stream Concurrency Efficiency

Efficiency of concurrent stream execution.

3.8.4 SCHED-004: Preemption Latency

Latency when higher-priority work preempts running kernels.

3.9 Fragmentation Metrics (FRAG-001 to FRAG-003)

3.9.1 FRAG-001: Fragmentation Index

Memory fragmentation after allocation/free cycles:

f​r​a​g=1−l​a​r​g​e​s​t​_​f​r​e​e​_​b​l​o​c​kt​o​t​a​l​_​f​r​e​e​_​m​e​m​o​r​yfrag=1-\frac{largest\_free\_block}{total\_free\_memory} (27)

3.9.2 FRAG-002: Allocation Latency Degradation

Increase in allocation latency with fragmentation.

3.9.3 FRAG-003: Memory Compaction Efficiency

Memory reclaimed after defragmentation operations.

3.10 Error Recovery Metrics (ERR-001 to ERR-003)

3.10.1 ERR-001: Error Detection Latency

Time to detect and report CUDA errors.

3.10.2 ERR-002: Error Recovery Time

Time to recover GPU to usable state after errors.

3.10.3 ERR-003: Graceful Degradation Score

Measures how well the system handles resource exhaustion without crashing. We induce memory exhaustion and measure:

s​c​o​r​e=w1⋅In​o​_​c​r​a​s​h+w2⋅Ie​r​r​o​r​_​r​e​t​u​r​n​e​d+w3⋅Ir​e​c​o​v​e​r​yscore=w_{1}\cdot I_{no\_crash}+w_{2}\cdot I_{error\_returned}+w_{3}\cdot I_{recovery} (28)

where In​o​_​c​r​a​s​hI_{no\_crash} indicates the process survived (weight 0.4), Ie​r​r​o​r​_​r​e​t​u​r​n​e​dI_{error\_returned} indicates proper CUDA error codes were returned (weight 0.3), and Ir​e​c​o​v​e​r​yI_{recovery} indicates subsequent allocations succeeded after freeing memory (weight 0.3). Score ranges from 0% (crash) to 100% (full graceful handling).

4 Framework Architecture

4.1 System Design

GPU-Virt-Bench follows a modular architecture enabling extensibility and reproducibility. Figure 1 illustrates the key components.

4.2 Component Description

CLI Interface (main.c): Parses command-line arguments, manages benchmark configuration, and orchestrates metric execution.

Metric Modules (src/metrics/*.cu): CUDA implementations of each benchmark category. Each module exports a standard interface for result collection.

Utilities:

  • •

    timing.c: High-precision timing using clock_gettime and CUDA events

  • •

    statistics.c: Statistical analysis (mean, median, percentiles, CV)

  • •

    report.c: Result formatting and export

  • •

    process.c: Multi-process test orchestration

4.3 Supported Systems

GPU-Virt-Bench supports four execution modes:

Note on MIG-Ideal: The mig mode generates simulated baseline values derived from NVIDIA MIG specifications and published benchmarks. It does not execute on actual MIG partitions. This enables comparison even on systems without MIG hardware, but results should be validated against real MIG measurements when possible.

4.4 Statistical Methodology

Each metric is measured over configurable iterations (default: 100) with warmup runs (default: 10). Statistics computed include:

  • •

    Mean (μ\mu)

  • •

    Standard deviation (σ\sigma)

  • •

    Median (P50)

  • •

    Percentiles: P95, P99

  • •

    Coefficient of variation (C​V=σ/μCV=\sigma/\mu)

4.5 MIG Comparison Baseline

Each metric includes expected MIG baseline values derived from hardware specifications and published benchmarks [2, 4]. We compute both signed deviation and absolute gap to indicate direction and magnitude:

For “higher is better” metrics:

ΔM​I​G=m​e​t​r​i​ca​c​t​u​a​l−m​e​t​r​i​cM​I​Gm​e​t​r​i​cM​I​G×100%\Delta_{MIG}=\frac{metric_{actual}-metric_{MIG}}{metric_{MIG}}\times 100\% (29)

For “lower is better” metrics:

ΔM​I​G=m​e​t​r​i​cM​I​G−m​e​t​r​i​ca​c​t​u​a​lm​e​t​r​i​cM​I​G×100%\Delta_{MIG}=\frac{metric_{MIG}-metric_{actual}}{metric_{MIG}}\times 100\% (30)

Positive ΔM​I​G\Delta_{MIG} indicates the software solution outperforms the MIG baseline; negative values indicate degradation. The “MIG parity” percentage reported in results represents the average normalized score across all metrics.

Note: MIG baselines in this evaluation are simulated from NVIDIA specifications and published benchmark data, not measured on actual MIG partitions. This represents an idealized upper bound; real MIG performance may vary based on partition geometry and workload characteristics.

5 Implementation Details

5.1 Overhead Measurement

Kernel launch latency (OH-001) measures the CPU-side overhead of the cuLaunchKernel API call, which includes virtualization layer interception. We use host-side high-resolution timers around a minimal kernel launch, followed by synchronization:

This measures the time for the launch call to return, which includes virtualization layer overhead (API interception, quota checks) but not kernel execution time. We subtract native baseline to isolate virtualization overhead.

To isolate API interception overhead (OH-005), we measure the same CUDA call under both native and virtualized execution, then compute the difference:

The difference between virtualized and native execution times isolates the overhead attributable to dlsym hook resolution, quota checking, and memory tracking—excluding the driver’s base cost.

6 Scoring Methodology

6.1 Per-Metric Scoring

Each metric is scored based on its relationship to expected (MIG baseline) values. All scores are normalized to [0,1][0,1]:

For “lower is better” metrics (e.g., latency, overhead):

s​c​o​r​e=min⁡(1,max⁡(0,e​x​p​e​c​t​e​da​c​t​u​a​l))score=\min\left(1,\max\left(0,\frac{expected}{actual}\right)\right) (31)

For “higher is better” metrics (e.g., throughput, accuracy):

s​c​o​r​e=min⁡(1,max⁡(0,a​c​t​u​a​le​x​p​e​c​t​e​d))score=\min\left(1,\max\left(0,\frac{actual}{expected}\right)\right) (32)

A score of 1.0 indicates performance equal to or better than the MIG baseline.

6.2 Category Aggregation

Category scores aggregate individual metrics:

s​c​o​r​ec​a​t​e​g​o​r​y=1n​∑i=1ns​c​o​r​eiscore_{category}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}score_{i} (33)

6.3 Overall Score and Grading

The overall score weights categories by their importance to production deployments:

s​c​o​r​eo​v​e​r​a​l​l=∑cwc×s​c​o​r​ecscore_{overall}=\sum_{c}w_{c}\times score_{c} (34)

8 Discussion

8.1 Software vs. Hardware Virtualization

Our results quantify the gap between software virtualization and hardware MIG. Key observations:

Overhead is significant but manageable: Software solutions add 10-20% throughput overhead for typical workloads. For latency-sensitive inference, this may be acceptable given the cost savings from better utilization.

Isolation is approximate: Software SM limiting achieves 85-93% accuracy versus MIG’s hardware guarantees. This is sufficient for many multi-tenant scenarios but may not meet strict SLA requirements.

LLM workloads are sensitive: Memory allocation patterns in LLM inference amplify virtualization overhead. Optimizations targeting KV cache operations yield significant benefits.

8.2 Practical Recommendations

Based on our evaluation:

  1. 1.

    Use MIG when available for strict isolation requirements

  2. 2.

    Prefer BUD-FCSP over HAMi-core for LLM inference

  3. 3.

    Monitor fairness metrics in multi-tenant deployments

  4. 4.

    Size memory limits conservatively to avoid enforcement overhead

8.3 Limitations

GPU-Virt-Bench has the following limitations that users should consider:

  • •

    Single-GPU focus: Current metrics target single-GPU scenarios; multi-GPU distributed training patterns require extension

  • •

    Synthetic workloads: LLM metrics use custom CUDA kernels rather than production frameworks (PyTorch, TensorRT-LLM); results should be validated against real workloads

  • •

    Simulated MIG baseline: MIG-Ideal values are derived from specifications, not measured on actual MIG partitions; real MIG performance varies by geometry and workload

  • •

    Limited GPU coverage: Evaluation was conducted on A100; behavior may differ on other GPU architectures

  • •

    Software version sensitivity: HAMi-core and BUD-FCSP implementations evolve; results reflect specific versions tested

9 Conclusion

GPU-Virt-Bench provides a comprehensive framework for evaluating GPU virtualization systems. Our 56-metric taxonomy covers overhead, isolation, and workload-specific performance dimensions. Through evaluation of HAMi-core and BUD-FCSP, we demonstrate that software virtualization achieves 72-85% of ideal MIG performance with acceptable overhead for many deployment scenarios.

The framework enables practitioners to make informed decisions about GPU resource sharing strategies and provides virtualization developers with actionable improvement targets. Future work will extend GPU-Virt-Bench to multi-GPU scenarios, incorporate additional virtualization backends, and develop automated regression testing for virtualization systems.
